name: Color treatment
controls: Which hues, values and saturations the piece uses, in what proportions, how they relate to each other, and how color itself changes over time.
question: What should the color feel like, and how strict should the palette be?
notes: Color treatment stacks along several independent axes: value range (black and white, grayscale), palette system (limited, brand, accent-color), character (pastel, muted, neon), harmony (complementary, analogous, triadic), surface color (gradient, mesh gradient, iridescent) and theme/contrast (dark UI, high contrast). Pick at most two, usually one system plus one character (e.g. accent-color system + muted). Terminology is loose in practice: 'monochrome' is used by most people to mean black and white, while strictly it means one hue at many values; 'neon' and 'fluorescent' are used interchangeably in briefs but describe emissive light versus reflective pigment; 'duotone' is often misused for any two-color palette. Harmony terms (complementary, analogous, triadic) come from color-wheel theory and describe hue relationships only; they say nothing about saturation or value, so pair them with a character option. Every prompt assumes text contrast of at least 4.5:1 against its immediate background (3:1 for display type 48px and larger) unless the option deliberately says otherwise. In a HyperFrames build, all color change is driven by tweens on the paused GSAP timeline (CSS custom properties, fill, background-color), never by CSS @keyframes or transitions.

options.what: The full-frame background tweens from one flat color to another to mark a new scene or idea.
options.prompt: Change scenes by tweening the stage background-color between palette colors over 600-900ms with power2.inOut; foreground ink recolors on the same tween so contrast never drops below 4.5:1 mid-transition. Never pass through a muddy midpoint: if two hues are far apart on the wheel, interpolate via a CSS custom property in oklch, or cut on a wipe instead.

options.what: A solid band of color sweeps across the frame, revealing the next state underneath or behind it.
options.prompt: Transition with a flat color wipe: a full-bleed rectangle in the accent color translates across the frame (clip-path inset or scaleX from a transform-origin edge) in 350-500ms with power3.inOut, holds 1-2 frames fully covering, then exits the opposite side revealing the new scene. Use a second, offset band in a support color 60-80ms behind for a layered wipe.

options.what: The stops, angle or positions of a gradient move slowly so the background feels alive without changing its palette.
options.prompt: Animate the background gradient slowly: register --g-angle and --g-stop as @property values and tween them on the timeline (angle 20-40 degrees and stop positions 10-20% over 6-10s, sine.inOut, yoyo). Or oversize the gradient layer to 200% and tween its background-position. Motion must be barely noticeable; no hue cycling.

options.what: Colors step or rotate through a sequence repeatedly, a technique with roots in 8-bit palette-cycling animation.
options.prompt: Cycle an element's fill through 3-5 palette colors on a fixed beat (every 250-500ms, stepped, no interpolation) or rotate hue continuously with filter: hue-rotate tweened 0-360deg over 4-8s linear. Restrict cycling to one element or a pattern; never cycle text or the full background.

options.what: A specific object changes color to signal a state change, selection or emphasis.
options.prompt: Signal state changes by recoloring the object only: tween fill or background-color from neutral to accent in 200-300ms with power2.out, optionally with a 1.04 scale pulse. Keep every other element static and neutral so the recolor is the only event on screen.

options.what: The whole composition swaps from one color theme to another, showing that the same layout carries several palettes.
options.prompt: Define the palette as CSS custom properties (--bg, --ink, --accent, --support) on the scene root and switch themes by tweening all four together over 500-700ms power2.inOut, or by a circular clip-path reveal of the new theme from the point of interaction. Layout, type and positions must not move during the swap.

options.what: The composition transforms between a light theme and a dark theme, usually to show a dark-mode feature or a mood shift.
options.prompt: Transform light to dark with a radial clip-path reveal (circle growing from the toggle to 150% of the frame diagonal over 700ms, power3.inOut) of an identical dark-themed copy. Dark theme uses #0f1115-style near-black surfaces, not pure black, with raised surfaces 4-8% lighter; accent desaturates 10-15% so it does not vibrate on dark.

options.what: Dominant, secondary and accent colors occupy roughly 60%, 30% and 10% of the frame.
options.prompt: Distribute color 60/30/10 by frame area: the background/dominant color covers about 60%, a secondary surface or ink color about 30%, and the accent about 10%, reserved for the focal element.

options.what: An almost entirely neutral frame in which the accent covers 10% or less and appears only at the focal point.
options.prompt: Keep at least 90% of every frame neutral (background, ink, grays). The accent covers 10% or less of the frame, appears on one element per shot, and moves with the story's focal point.

options.what: Two to four colors share the frame in large, roughly equal fields with no single dominant color.
options.prompt: Divide the frame into 2-4 large flat color fields of roughly equal area with hard edges; no field under 15% of the frame. Type sits on whichever field gives 4.5:1 contrast.

options.what: A palette built from one hue at many lightness and saturation steps, with no second hue.
options.looks: Every element is a tint or shade of one hue, for example navy through powder blue; hierarchy comes entirely from value; surfaces separate by lightness steps of 8-12%.
options.motion: Value shifts carry emphasis: an element brightens or darkens to become focal; scene changes move the whole ramp lighter or darker.
options.use: Brand films built on one signature color, calm explainers, technical product pieces, sections of a larger film that need a pause.
options.conveys: Cohesion, calm, control; a strong single-brand presence.
options.vs: Strictly, monochrome means one hue; in common usage it also means black and white. Grayscale is monochrome with zero saturation. Duotone maps an image's values onto two colors.
options.prompt: Use a strictly monochromatic palette built on one hue: darkest step for background or ink, lightest for the other, 2-3 intermediate steps for surfaces and secondary shapes. No second hue anywhere, including shadows (tint shadows with the same hue). Build hierarchy with value only: the focal element takes the highest contrast step against its surroundings; body text keeps 4.5:1.

options.what: Pure black and pure (or near-pure) white only, with no intermediate grays.
options.looks: Hard two-value frames: black type on white or the reverse; shapes are solid silhouettes; tone, if needed, comes from pattern (halftone, hatching) rather than gray fill.
options.motion: Inversions are the main device: a frame flips polarity on a beat; shapes wipe from black to white; hard cuts feel sharp because there is no gradation.
options.use: Typographic statements, fashion and editorial brand films, developer tools, manifesto films, stark title cards.
options.vs: Grayscale uses the full continuous gray ramp; black and white allows only the two extremes. 'Monochrome' is often said when black and white is meant.
options.prompt: Use only two values: #0a0a0a and #fafafa. No grays, no tints, no shadows or soft gradients. If tone is needed, render it as a pattern (halftone dots or line hatching) in the same black. Use polarity inversion (swap background and ink in a single frame or a hard wipe) as the scene-change device, on beats.

options.what: A palette of neutral grays from near-black to near-white with no hue at all.
options.looks: Soft, even tonal ranges; UI and objects rendered in 5-9 gray steps; often paired with a single accent that becomes very loud by comparison.
options.motion: Emphasis by lifting an element's value or adding the only color on screen; desaturation of footage or UI to push it into the background.
options.use: Wireframe-style explainers, architectural and technical pieces, 'before' states in before/after, backgrounds for an accent-color system.
options.conveys: Neutrality, restraint, a blueprint or draft quality; can read as muted or clinical if unaccented.
options.vs: Black and white uses only the extremes; grayscale uses the whole ramp. Monochrome keeps a hue; grayscale has zero saturation.
options.prompt: Render everything in true neutral grays (zero saturation) on a 5-step ramp: #111111, #3a3a3a, #8a8a8a, #d4d4d4, #f4f4f4. Background uses an end step; surfaces separate by one step; text uses the opposite end for 4.5:1 or better. Do not tint grays warm or cool. Footage and screenshots are desaturated to 0% with CSS filter: grayscale(1).

options.what: An image or scene whose tonal values are mapped onto a ramp between two colors: one for shadows, one for highlights.
options.looks: Photos and UI screenshots rendered as, for example, deep indigo shadows blending into coral highlights; full tonal detail survives, but only two hues exist, with their blends between.
options.motion: Duotone footage or photos pan and scale inside frames; the two mapped colors can tween together to re-grade a scene; hard cuts between differently mapped images.
options.use: Campaign and event graphics, music and culture brands, editorial brand films, photo-led social content (the Spotify 2015-era campaign look).
options.conveys: Bold graphic identity, energy, editorial confidence; turns mixed photography into one coherent system.
options.vs: Two-color palette: two flat spot colors used side by side, with no tonal mapping. Duotone is a process applied to continuous-tone images. Tritone adds a third mapped color.
options.prompt: Apply a duotone to all photography and footage: map shadows to #1b1446 and highlights to #ff6b57. In the browser use an SVG filter (feColorMatrix to luminance, then feComponentTransfer with table values for each channel) or a grayscale image under a highlight-color layer with mix-blend-mode: multiply and a shadow-color layer with screen. Type is set in the light neutral #f7efe6 or the shadow color, never a third hue.

options.what: A deliberately small, fixed set of three to five colors used for everything in the piece.
options.looks: Every shape, type element and background drawn from the same few colors; no ad-hoc tints; strong visual unity across scenes.
options.motion: Colors swap roles between scenes (background becomes ink); objects recolor between the fixed set; transitions reuse palette colors as wipe fills.
options.use: Illustrated explainers, brand motion systems, print-inspired pieces (risograph, screen print), social series.
options.conveys: Craft and intention; a designed, art-directed feel.
options.vs: Brand palette is dictated by guidelines; a limited palette is a stylistic restraint and can be invented for the piece. Color blocking is about how large the fields are, not how many colors.
options.prompt: Use exactly four colors and no others: background #f3ece0, ink #1e2a3a, accent #e4572e, support #76b041. No tints, opacities or gradients to invent in-between colors; overlaps use a palette color, not a blend. Roles may swap between scenes (ink becomes background) but the set never grows.

options.what: The client's documented brand colors, applied with their defined roles and ratios.
options.looks: Primary brand color recognisable within the first second; secondary colors in support roles; neutrals from the brand system; nothing off-brand.
options.motion: Brand color used for the most important motion moments (logo resolve, key reveal); transitions often wipe in the primary color.
options.use: Any piece for an established brand: launch films, idents, social content, product demos.
options.vs: Accent-color system is a structure (neutral frame, rationed accent) that a brand palette can be poured into; brand palette only says where the colors come from.
options.prompt: Use the brand's documented palette only (from the brand kit or captured site tokens): map primary to the hero moments and logo resolve, secondary colors to supporting shapes, brand neutrals to backgrounds and body text. Keep the brand's stated ratio if one exists, otherwise 60/30/10 neutral/secondary/primary. Do not invent new hues; any tint must be a documented brand tint. Check every text pairing for 4.5:1 and swap to the brand neutral where the brand color fails.

options.what: A neutral frame (black, white, grays) with one saturated accent color reserved for the thing that matters.
options.looks: Near-monochrome scenes where one button, word, line or data point is the only color; the eye goes straight to it.
options.motion: The accent moves with the story: it hands off from element to element, recolors the active state, draws the one line on the chart.
options.use: SaaS launch films, product demos, data stories, developer tools; the default for contemporary product motion.
options.conveys: Clarity, focus, confidence; the product feels precise.
options.vs: Limited palette uses several equal colors; an accent system has one loud color and neutrals. Black and white has no accent.
search: neutral palette accent color UI animation
options.prompt: Build every frame from neutrals (#0e0e10 ink, #f5f5f4 background, #a1a1aa secondary) plus one accent, #ff4f1a. The accent covers no more than 10% of the frame and appears on exactly one element per shot: the active state, the key word, the single highlighted data series. When focus moves, the accent moves: recolor the old element to neutral as the new one takes the accent, in 200-300ms. Never use the accent for decoration or backgrounds.

options.what: Red, yellow and blue (plus black and white) used as flat, pure color fields.
options.looks: Pure red, yellow, blue shapes on white or off-white with black lines; geometric; each color has an equal claim to attention.
options.motion: Geometric shapes slide, rotate and snap into compositions; colors swap between shapes on beats.
options.use: Bauhaus and De Stijl-inspired brand motion, educational content, children's products, playful tech.
options.conveys: Directness, play, foundational clarity, modernist heritage.
options.vs: High saturation covers any vivid hues; primary colors are specifically red, yellow, blue. Triadic is the general color-wheel relationship; primaries are one triadic set.
options.prompt: Use flat primaries only: red #e1261c, yellow #f7c325, blue #1d4fa3 on off-white #f4f1ea with #111111 for type and lines. No tints, gradients or shadows. Give each primary a distinct shape role (e.g. red circles, yellow triangles, blue squares). Yellow never carries text; set type in black.

options.what: The frame is divided into large, hard-edged fields of solid color that act as the composition itself.
options.looks: Two to four big flat panels meeting at hard edges; type and objects sit inside fields; no gradients; the layout reads from across a room.
options.motion: Fields slide, split and resize to re-compose the frame; each new scene arrives as a field wiping over the last.
options.use: Social ads, campaign animation, fashion and retail motion, bold brand films, split-screen comparisons.
options.conveys: Energy, confidence, graphic boldness, fashion sensibility.
options.vs: Limited palette is about how many colors; color blocking is about how color is laid out (large fields). A color wipe is a transition; color blocking is a static layout principle that can use wipes.
options.prompt: Compose each frame from 2-4 large, flat, hard-edged color fields (#ff5a36, #2b59c3, #ffd23f, with #111111 and #f7f3ea for type); no field smaller than 15% of the frame, no gradients or shadows. Re-compose between scenes by sliding and resizing fields along the grid (400-600ms, power3.inOut), never by fading. Type sits within one field and takes whichever of black or off-white gives 4.5:1.

options.what: High-lightness, low-to-medium saturation hues such as mint, peach, lavender and butter yellow.
options.looks: Light, airy fields and shapes; soft contrast between colors; usually paired with dark ink for legible type.
options.motion: Gentle, springy or floaty motion; soft color crossfades; nothing harsh.
options.use: Consumer apps, wellness, lifestyle and beauty, playful tech, onboarding animations, kawaii and soft-3D styles.
options.vs: Muted colors are lower in saturation but not necessarily light; pastels are always light. Low contrast is a property of pairings; pastels only become low-contrast when pastel text sits on pastel ground.
options.prompt: Use pastel fields (mint #bfe8d8, peach #ffc9b5, lavender #d9ccff) on a warm off-white #fff6ec. All text and fine lines use the dark ink #2a2540 to keep 4.5:1; pastel never carries text. Keep neighboring pastels close in lightness so no single field shouts; emphasis comes from the ink, scale or motion rather than a louder color.

options.what: Hues pulled toward gray: reduced saturation across the whole palette, at any lightness.
options.looks: Dusty blue, sage, clay, slate; sophisticated and quiet; colors sit together without vibrating.
options.motion: Slow, considered easing; long holds; color changes are subtle value shifts rather than hue jumps.
options.use: Premium and editorial brand films, finance and professional services, documentary-style pieces, calm product stories.
options.vs: Pastel is light and soft; muted can be dark or mid-tone. Earth tones are a specific muted family (browns, ochres, olives). Low contrast concerns value difference, not saturation.
options.prompt: Desaturate the whole palette: keep every hue under roughly 35% saturation (slate #7d8f99, sage #a8b39a, clay #c28e74) on a warm neutral #eeeae3 with charcoal #2f3437 ink. No fully saturated color anywhere, including the accent; emphasis comes from value contrast, not saturation. Color changes are slow (600ms+) and small.

options.what: Warm, muted hues drawn from soil, clay, wood, stone and plants: terracotta, ochre, olive, umber, sand.
options.looks: Warm browns and oranges with olive greens on sand or cream; often paired with paper texture and serif type.
options.motion: Organic, unhurried motion; growth and unfolding metaphors; soft crossfades.
options.use: Sustainability and climate brands, food, craft and outdoor products, wellness, heritage and editorial pieces.
options.vs: Muted is any desaturated palette; earth tones are a warm, nature-derived subset. Warm palette can be bright (reds, oranges); earth tones are always subdued.
options.prompt: Use an earth-tone palette: sand #f1e7d6 background, umber #3b2a20 ink, terracotta #c0623b as the accent, ochre #d19c3c and olive #6b7a3f in support. No cool blues or pure grays; any neutral is warm. Pair with slight paper grain if texture is allowed.

options.what: Hues at or near full chroma used across the palette, not just as an accent.
options.looks: Vivid, punchy fields and shapes; strong color contrast; saturated colors placed next to each other with black or white separating them to control vibration.
options.motion: Fast, energetic motion; beat-synced color swaps; bold wipes.
options.use: Social ads, youth and entertainment brands, music, sports, playful tech, pop-art styles.
options.vs: Neon adds emissive glow on dark ground; fluorescent refers to pigments that exceed normal saturation. High saturation is just vivid color, no glow implied.
options.prompt: Use fully saturated hues (#ff2e63, #08d9d6, #ffd000) as large fields and shapes, separated by black #0d0d0d or white #ffffff so saturated colors do not touch edge-to-edge in fine detail (it vibrates). Text is only black or white. Avoid more than three saturated hues in one frame.

options.what: Saturated hues rendered as if emitting light, with glow halos, almost always on a dark background.
options.looks: Magenta, cyan, electric green lines and type glowing against near-black; bright cores with soft colored halos; tube-sign or synthwave quality.
options.motion: Flicker-on ignition, pulsing glow, light tracing along strokes, beat-synced intensity.
options.use: Nightlife, gaming, music, cyberpunk and synthwave styles, event openers, tech launches at night.
options.conveys: Nightlife energy, futurism, excitement, retro-futuristic cool.
options.vs: Fluorescent is a pigment on a light surface (highlighter ink) with no glow; neon is emissive light. High saturation has no glow.
options.prompt: Set neon strokes and type (#ff2bd6, #21e6ff, #b3ff3a) on near-black #07060d. Build each glow from a light core (the color mixed 40% toward white) plus 2-3 stacked drop-shadows or text-shadows of the pure color at 4px, 12px and 32px blur; never glow body copy. Ignite elements with a 2-3 frame stepped flicker then a 200ms ease to full. Use at most two neon hues per frame.

options.what: Ultra-bright pigment colors (safety orange, highlighter yellow, hot pink) printed or painted on light surfaces, with no glow.
options.looks: Flat, almost vibrating fields of fluorescent pink, orange or yellow-green on white or paper, often with black type; print and poster quality.
options.motion: Snappy flat-graphic motion, stickers slapping on, highlighter strokes swiping across words.
options.use: Streetwear and youth brands, zine and punk styles, risograph-inspired motion, sale and announcement graphics, highlighting in editorial motion.
options.conveys: Urgency, attitude, youth, DIY print energy.
options.vs: Neon is emissive light on dark; fluorescent is reflective pigment on light. Risograph fluorescent pink is a well-known spot ink in this family.
options.prompt: Use fluorescent flat fills (pink #ff48b0, orange #ff7a1a, yellow-green #d6ff3f) on paper white #fbfbf7 with black #111111 type. No glow, blur or gradients. Use fluorescent color as a highlighter swipe behind key words (a skewed rectangle scaling from left in 250ms) or as large flat shapes; never set text in fluorescent on white (fails contrast).

options.what: A palette weighted toward reds, oranges, yellows and warm neutrals.
options.looks: Cream and sand backgrounds, orange and red accents, warm grays; shadows tinted brown rather than gray.
options.motion: Inviting, human motion; gentle easing; growth and glow metaphors.
options.use: Consumer products, food, hospitality, community and human-centred brand films, onboarding.
options.vs: Earth tones are warm but muted; a warm palette can be vivid. Cool palette is its opposite temperature.
options.prompt: Weight the palette warm: cream #fff4e6 background, deep brown #2b1a12 ink, orange #ff7b39 primary accent with gold #f2b544 and red #d9412b in support. Tint every neutral and shadow warm (brown-gray, not blue-gray). No blues or cool grays except as a deliberate single contrast element.

options.what: A palette weighted toward blues, teals, violets and cool grays.
options.looks: Blue-gray backgrounds, teal and blue accents, violet support; crisp and clean; shadows tinted blue.
options.motion: Precise, smooth, controlled motion; data and system metaphors.
options.use: Fintech, security, healthcare, enterprise SaaS, developer tools, technical explainers.
options.vs: Monochrome blue uses one hue; a cool palette mixes several cool hues. Warm palette is its opposite temperature.
options.prompt: Weight the palette cool: blue-white #f2f6fa background, deep navy #0d1b2a ink, blue #2f6fed primary with teal #19b3a6 and violet #7b6cf6 as support. Tint neutrals and shadows cool (blue-gray). If an alert or error color is required, it is the only warm hue on screen.

options.what: Two hues from opposite sides of the color wheel (blue/orange, purple/yellow, red/green) used together for maximum hue contrast.
options.looks: One hue dominates, its opposite punctuates; strong tension and pop; at equal amounts and saturation it vibrates.
options.motion: Push-pull devices: the complement flashes in for emphasis, before/after states in opposite hues.
options.use: Sports, entertainment and social graphics, comparisons (A vs B), bold brand films.
options.vs: Split-complementary uses the two neighbors of the complement for less tension. Analogous is the opposite strategy (neighboring hues).
options.prompt: Build a complementary scheme: blue #1f4fd1 dominant (about 60-70% of colored area) on deep navy #0f1e3d, with orange #ff8a1f as the complement, limited to 10-15% on focal elements. Never place the two at equal saturation and area, and never let fine type in one sit on the other (it vibrates); type is #f4f4f0 or navy.

options.what: Three or so neighboring hues on the color wheel (e.g. yellow, orange, red) used together.
options.looks: Harmonious, low-tension color that flows; often expressed as smooth gradients between neighbors.
options.motion: Smooth color drift between neighbors; gradients slowly shifting; calm, cohesive scene changes.
options.use: Ambient backgrounds, wellness and lifestyle, sunset/ocean themes, brand films needing warmth or calm.
options.vs: Monochrome uses a single hue; analogous spans adjacent hues. Complementary uses opposites.
options.prompt: Use an analogous scheme spanning about 60 degrees of hue: magenta-red #b3204d, orange-red #ef5b3b, amber #f7a531, anchored by a dark #2a0f1f and a light #fff1dc for type. Transitions drift along this hue range rather than jumping outside it. Add value contrast deliberately, since analogous hues alone give weak hierarchy.

options.what: Three hues evenly spaced (120 degrees apart) on the color wheel.
options.looks: Lively, balanced variety; typically one dominant hue with two supporting, often slightly muted to avoid a carnival look.
options.motion: Each hue gets a role (category, character, state); swaps between categories use recolors.
options.use: Illustrated explainers, playful brands, category-coded data, children's and education products.
options.vs: Primary colors are one specific triad (red, yellow, blue). Tetradic uses four hues. Complementary uses two.
options.prompt: Use a triadic scheme: red #e0475b, blue #3aa0e0, yellow #f2c230 on off-white #fbf8f2 with #1c1c28 ink. One hue dominates (about 60% of colored area), the other two share the rest. Assign each hue a stable meaning (e.g. a category or a character) and keep it for the whole piece.

options.what: A smooth blend between two or more colors along one axis (linear) or from a point outward (radial or conic).
options.looks: Backgrounds, shapes or type filled with smooth color transitions, e.g. violet to blue; the dominant look of 2013-2020 app and SaaS marketing.
options.motion: Gradient angles rotate, stops slide, gradients sweep across type as a sheen; backgrounds slowly shift.
options.use: Landing-page heroes, app promos, tech brand films, backgrounds behind UI.
options.conveys: Modernity, energy, digital polish; can read dated or generic if overused.
options.vs: Mesh gradient blends many colors in two dimensions from a grid of points; a regular gradient blends along one axis or radius. Analogous is a hue relationship that gradients often express.
options.prompt: Fill the background with a linear gradient at 135 degrees from #5b3df5 to #2fa4ff, darkening to #0b0b1a at the far edge for depth. Interpolate in oklch (linear-gradient(in oklch, ...)) to avoid a gray midpoint. Keep gradients to backgrounds and at most one hero shape; UI and type stay flat. Animate by tweening the angle 20-30 degrees over 8s with sine.inOut via an @property custom property.

options.what: A two-dimensional gradient in which color comes from many points on a grid or freely placed blobs, blending in all directions.
options.looks: Soft, organic color clouds: pools of violet, peach and teal melting into each other with no single direction; the 'aurora' background of contemporary SaaS sites.
options.motion: Color pools drift slowly, merge and separate; the whole field breathes; often the only moving thing behind static UI.
options.use: SaaS and AI product heroes, launch-film backgrounds, app promos, ambient loops.
options.conveys: Softness, fluidity, contemporary tech polish, an AI or generative feel.
options.vs: A regular gradient blends along one axis; a mesh gradient blends across a surface from many points. Iridescent color depends on viewing angle; a mesh gradient is fixed color placed in space.
options.prompt: Build a mesh gradient background on #0d0a1f: 4-5 absolutely positioned circles (each 50-80% of frame width) filled with #7b5cff, #ff8fb1, #35d0c9 and #ffd6a5, blurred with filter: blur(80-120px) inside a container with overflow: hidden, plus 4-6% grain on top to prevent banding. Drift each blob on its own slow path (x/y 10-20% of frame over 8-12s, sine.inOut, yoyo) on the paused timeline. For true mesh fidelity use a canvas or WebGL shader. UI sits on top with solid surfaces.

options.what: Color that shifts smoothly across the spectrum depending on viewing angle, like a soap bubble, pearl or oil film.
options.looks: Soft, continuous hue drift (pink to teal to gold) across a surface, strongest at edges and highlights; pale and luminous rather than rainbow-striped.
options.motion: Hues slide across surfaces as objects rotate or light moves; subtle shimmer.
options.use: Beauty and fashion, premium consumer tech, Y2K and soft-3D styles, AI product branding.
options.vs: Holographic is diffraction: sharp, banded spectral rainbows and sparkle; iridescent is interference: smooth, pastel, angle-dependent drift. Mesh gradients are static color; iridescence responds to angle.
options.prompt: Render iridescent surfaces with a conic-gradient cycling pale pink #ffc6e0, aqua #b8f1f0, gold #fbe7b5 and lilac #c9b8ff, layered under a soft white radial highlight, applied only to hero objects and type, never the whole frame. Tie the gradient rotation (--iri-angle) to the object's rotation or tilt so hue shifts as it turns (about 90 degrees of hue per 30 degrees of rotation). Keep saturation low; iridescence is pale.

options.what: Diffractive rainbow color with sharp spectral bands and sparkle, like holographic foil or trading-card holos.
options.looks: Vivid spectral stripes (red through violet) sweeping across a surface, often with a fine pattern or glitter; chrome-like under the rainbow.
options.motion: Rainbow bands sweep across as the object tilts; sparkle points twinkle; foil sheen passes over type.
options.use: Y2K and rave aesthetics, music and fashion campaigns, collectibles, premium packaging reveals, crypto and web3 branding.
options.conveys: Excitement, futurism, collectible value, nostalgia for 2000s pop.
options.vs: Iridescent is smooth and pastel (interference); holographic is banded and saturated (diffraction). Chrome is neutral reflection with no rainbow.
options.prompt: Render holographic foil: a silver base #c7c9d1 overlaid with a repeating-linear-gradient of saturated spectral bands (#ff5ea8, #ffe45e, #5effc2, #5ec8ff) at 20-30% band width, mix-blend-mode: color-dodge or overlay, plus a fine diagonal line pattern at 8% opacity. Sweep the band position with the object's tilt (background-position tweened with rotation). Use on one hero object or wordmark only.

options.what: Near-black backgrounds with light type, elevation expressed by lighter surfaces rather than shadows.
options.looks: #0b0d10-style backgrounds, surfaces 4-8% lighter per elevation step, off-white text, one luminous accent; the look of developer tools and pro apps.
options.motion: Light emerges from dark: glows, gradients and accents fade up; UI surfaces lift by lightening.
options.use: Developer tools, AI products, pro creative software, launch films, night-time and cinematic moods.
options.conveys: Focus, power-user seriousness, premium tech, drama.
options.vs: High contrast is about value difference and can be light or dark; dark UI is a theme with moderate, eye-friendly contrast (off-white on near-black, not pure white on pure black). Neon is a color character that often lives on dark UI.
options.prompt: Use a dark theme: background #0b0d10, surface #16191e, raised surface #23272e, text #e6e8eb (never pure white on pure black), secondary text at 60-65% opacity, one accent #6e8bff desaturated enough not to vibrate. Express elevation by lighter surfaces and a 1px top border at rgba(255,255,255,0.06), not by drop shadows. Accent glows sparingly at 20-30% opacity.

options.what: White or off-white backgrounds with dark type, elevation expressed by soft shadows and borders.
options.looks: Clean white or warm off-white canvases, gray hairline borders, soft shadows, dark ink; the default of most SaaS marketing.
options.motion: UI cards lift with growing shadows; clean slides and scales; color stays in the accent.
options.use: SaaS launch films, product demos, onboarding, fintech and productivity tools.
options.vs: High contrast pushes to pure black on pure white; light UI usually uses softer #111-on-#fafafa. Pastel is a color character that can sit inside a light UI.
options.prompt: Use a light theme: canvas #fafaf9, cards #ffffff with 1px #e7e5e4 borders and a soft shadow (0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,0.04), 0 8px 24px rgba(0,0,0,0.06)), ink #18181b, secondary text #57534e, accent #4f46e5 only on active and key elements. Show elevation changes by tweening shadow spread and a 2-4px lift.

options.what: Large value differences between foreground and background everywhere, well beyond minimum legibility.
options.looks: Black on white or white on black, bold fills, hard edges, little midtone; every element reads instantly.
options.motion: Hard cuts, polarity flips, snap transitions; motion reads clearly even at small sizes and on phones.
options.use: Social video (autoplay on mobile), neo-brutalist and editorial pieces, accessibility-first content, typographic statements.
options.vs: Black and white is a palette; high contrast is a property any palette can have (e.g. yellow on black). Dark UI is intentionally lower contrast than this.
options.prompt: Keep all foreground/background pairings at 7:1 or higher (pure #000000 and #ffffff, with #ffe600 as a single accent used only on black). No midtone grays, soft shadows or low-opacity text. Separate every element from its neighbor by a strong value step; change scenes by polarity flips or hard wipes.

options.what: Deliberately small value differences, with elements distinguished by subtle tone-on-tone shifts.
options.looks: Beige on cream, gray on gray, embossed-looking forms; quiet, sophisticated, hazy; only the key text breaks the tonal range.
options.motion: Slow, soft motion; elements emerge gently from the ground; depth by subtle shadow and highlight.
options.use: Luxury, fashion, architecture and interiors, calm ambient loops, neumorphic and soft-UI styles.
options.vs: Muted is low saturation; low contrast is low value difference; they often travel together but are independent. Low contrast must still keep readable text at 4.5:1; the rule applies to shapes and surfaces, not copy.
options.prompt: Keep shapes and surfaces within a narrow value band: background #ece6dc, surfaces #e2dacd and #d3c9b8, separated by soft shadows and highlights rather than outlines or color. Only text breaks the band: set it in #3d352c for at least 4.5:1. No accents above low saturation; motion is slow (700ms+) so forms seem to rise out of the ground.
